profile.reading:
This is Digital Realty facility IAD37, at 44060 Digital Loudoun Plaza (Bldg K), Ashburn, VA 20147. Digital Realty's own property page for IAD37, fetched this session, lists the building at 280,000 square feet.

Digital Realty Trust is a publicly traded real estate investment trust (NYSE: DLR), SEC filer CIK 1297996, headquartered at 2323 Bryan Street, Dallas, Texas. As of December 31, 2025, the company reported 310 data centers worldwide, 221 wholly owned or consolidated and 89 held through unconsolidated joint ventures, totaling about 57.6 million rentable square feet across more than 55 metro markets, including 118 data centers in the United States, per its FY2025 Form 10-K filed with the SEC. Digital Realty operates as a colocation and wholesale landlord, leasing data center space and power to enterprise and cloud tenants rather than running its own compute, distinguishing it from hyperscaler operators such as AWS, Google, or Meta that are also tracked in this registry.

This building sits within Digital Realty's Northern Virginia campus, concentrated in Ashburn, Sterling, and Reston across Loudoun and Fairfax counties, part of the data center corridor the industry calls Data Center Alley. Digital Realty's own Northern Virginia metro page, fetched this session, lists at least 15 named properties across that campus totaling several million square feet, with individual buildings ranging from under 150,000 to more than 1 million square feet each; this is one of Digital Realty's largest single-metro concentrations globally. The company does not publish a consolidated IT power rating in megawatts for individual Northern Virginia buildings in the sources reviewed this session.

Digital Realty markets its interconnection and colocation product across this campus under its PlatformDIGITAL brand, positioning Northern Virginia alongside its other major North American hubs (Chicago, Dallas, Silicon Valley, and New York/New Jersey, also tracked in this registry) as core nodes in its global data center platform. The company's FY2025 10-K identifies the United States as its largest single national market by both facility count and rentable square footage.

profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley and extending into Prince William, Fairfax, and neighboring counties. Digital Realty is one of the corridor's founding colocation operators, alongside Equinix, and the area also hosts large single-tenant campuses for AWS, Microsoft, Google, and Meta, all tracked elsewhere in this registry. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, drawing network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout, and local zoning and grid-capacity disputes have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s.

reading.body:
IAD37 publishes 500 MW of IT capacity, making it the largest single facility among Virginia's 19 data centers with disclosed power figures and accounting for roughly 38 percent of their combined published load.

The 500 MW figure is an upper bound on compute density, not a statement of current utilization. At 40 kW per rack, a density typical of AI training clusters, this translates to roughly 12,500 racks or approximately 1.25 million accelerator card slots. At 10 kW per rack, a legacy enterprise density, the same power budget yields 50,000 racks. Digital Realty publishes neither rack count nor per-rack power envelope, so the actual compute housed here and its workload mix remain opaque.

The facility occupies 280,000 square feet within Digital Realty's Northern Virginia campus, which spans multiple buildings across Ashburn, Loudoun, and surrounding counties. This campus concentration matters for power distribution and cooling because a single operator can optimize infrastructure across adjacent buildings rather than managing isolated sites. The 2N+2 cooling redundancy reported here is a reliability claim about how the facility handles equipment failures, not a measure of thermal efficiency or total cooling capacity.

Virginia's 326 mapped facilities show what opacity dominates this market. Only 19 publish capacity figures at all. The state's actual installed base of compute infrastructure is substantially larger than these numbers reflect, and the distribution of AI workloads within it cannot be derived from power figures alone.
